frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains a vital market for Algerian gas, creating leverage but also exposure to demand shifts, price volatility, and pressure for expanded foreign investment.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Libya, and Niger complicates border control and limits Algeria's ability to shape regional security without becoming directly entangled.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Angola remains heavily dependent on offshore oil revenues, leaving national finances vulnerable to production declines, price shocks, and the bargaining power of multinational operators.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-linked external debt
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure has expanded transport capacity but continues to shape fiscal priorities and constrain policy flexibility through debt and project-finance obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Niger trade disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger and border restrictions have disrupted traditional transit routes, increasing pressure on Cotonou's port economy and regional commercial diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel militant spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and recruitment risks in northern Benin threaten transport corridors, protected areas, and new investment in frontier infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers bargaining leverage
frictionVectors.details: Diamond-sector negotiations remain central to Botswana's fiscal autonomy, with uncertainty over marketing arrangements and mine investment affecting national revenue control.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals offers diversification but could reproduce enclave extraction unless local processing and procurement requirements are strengthened.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state influence over industrial and artisanal gold, but smuggling, informal production, and insecurity continue to divert value away from public institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Closer security ties with Russia may reduce reliance on Western partners, but opaque arrangements and operational dependence create new risks for strategic autonomy and civilian oversight.

highlights: Critical minerals under tighter state scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control over gold, rare-earth and nickel projects, but limited capital and technical capacity leave room for opaque foreign-linked deals.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border and logistics friction
frictionVectors.details: Political and security tensions with Rwanda disrupt cross-border commerce and complicate access to regional corridors and eastern DRC markets.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport and digital-connectivity projects rely heavily on European, Chinese and other external financing, creating long-term leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime-security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde’s Atlantic position attracts security cooperation and investment, while illegal fishing, trafficking and dependence on foreign maritime capabilities limit full sovereign control of its waters.

frictionVectors.title: Energy-sector external leverage
frictionVectors.details: International oil, gas and mining firms remain central to production and financing, while pipeline and LNG infrastructure expose the state to commercial and geopolitical bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside Boko Haram-related insecurity in the Far North, threatens roads, plantations and energy corridors while increasing reliance on external security support.

highlights: Gold and diamonds remain weakly governed

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-resources model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security structures retain influence around regime protection and mining areas, reducing transparency and limiting Bangui’s independent control over strategic resource concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridors and armed groups
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond production is concentrated in insecure zones where armed groups, foreign buyers and informal networks capture value outside effective state regulation.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues and export infrastructure remain central to public finances, leaving the state vulnerable to foreign operators, price shifts and disputes over production terms.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict, Sahel instability and the repositioning of French and other Western forces increase pressure on Chad to balance sovereignty claims with reliance on external intelligence, logistics and security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, limiting Comoros' territorial claims and shaping migration, security, and maritime policy. The dispute continues to constrain sovereignty without a near-term diplomatic breakthrough.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence in Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Ports, telecommunications, and energy infrastructure remain dependent on external finance and operators. This limits the government's ability to convert maritime resources and logistics into independent revenue.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in eastern Congo continues to erode state authority and expose the country to pressure from neighboring states and external security actors. Control of borderlands and mineral corridors remains fragmented.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and other minerals attract Chinese, Western, and regional competition, while weak enforcement enables opaque contracts and informal extraction. Kinshasa is seeking greater value capture but still lacks consistent control across production zones.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil companies and commodity-price exposure continue to shape public finances and limit diversification. State participation provides leverage, but governance and transparency concerns weaken sovereign control over rents.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and other external financing remain important to roads, ports, and urban projects. Debt obligations and project opacity can narrow policy autonomy even when infrastructure capacity improves.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Supply-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire remains exposed to foreign processors, traders, and regulatory requirements in its dominant cocoa sector. Efforts to expand domestic processing and farmer income are improving leverage but have not displaced external market power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, logistics, energy, and telecommunications attract substantial foreign investment, supporting growth while creating dependence on external operators and capital. Abidjan is balancing openness with efforts to retain regulatory and fiscal control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Presence
frictionVectors.details: Multiple foreign military facilities provide revenue and security but constrain Djibouti's strategic autonomy. Competition among external powers increases bargaining leverage while raising the risk of entanglement.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on port logistics, military rents, and external infrastructure finance. Debt obligations and foreign-linked terminal operations limit the state's ability to capture the full value of its geographic position.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to treat Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam as a strategic water-security threat. Negotiations remain vulnerable to unilateral operating decisions and wider tensions involving Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Asset Sales
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, Gulf deposits, and investment in state-linked assets provide liquidity but increase outside leverage over Egypt's fiscal and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Declining Oil and Gas Output
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and limited diversification are reducing the state's resource base, while foreign technical and financial partners retain importance in offshore production and LNG operations.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy facilities, and special economic projects remain dependent on external contractors and financing, creating exposure to Chinese, Western, and regional commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopian Red Sea Access
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's control of the Assab and Massawa coastline remains central to its security posture as Ethiopia seeks reliable maritime access. Any coercive move could internationalize an already tense border environment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc revenues support state autonomy, but production depends on foreign operators, capital, and export channels that limit fully sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: SACU and South African Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Customs receipts, imports, logistics, and market access are heavily tied to South Africa and the wider Southern African Customs Union, leaving Eswatini vulnerable to regional shocks and policy pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Diplomatic Recognition Contest
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's formal relationship with Taiwan brings development and technical support but also exposes the kingdom to pressure from China and changing Western engagement.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's electricity and bargaining position, but unresolved operating arrangements continue to generate acute friction with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Access and External Finance
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for dependable maritime access intersects with Somalia, Somaliland, Eritrea, and Gulf interests. Debt restructuring and dependence on Chinese and other external infrastructure finance further constrain strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Concession renegotiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese, oil, and timber while managing investor concerns. Chinese and French commercial interests remain deeply embedded in key sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors for manganese and other minerals rely on concentrated rail and port infrastructure, limiting bargaining power despite stronger state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets and weak monitoring continue to threaten coastal fisheries, a major food and livelihood asset. Enforcement capacity remains below the level needed to secure national waters.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and fiscal dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on external financing for roads, energy, and public investment, giving donors and regional partners significant policy leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining damages water systems and weakens formal state control over mineral rents. Foreign-linked supply chains and local political protection complicate enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more domestic processing and better terms for lithium and other minerals, but financing needs and external commodity markets limit its negotiating room.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou external consortiums
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project promises transformational revenue but is controlled through large foreign-backed consortiums and complex infrastructure commitments. Guinea must convert export growth into durable domestic industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Transition legitimacy and mining access
frictionVectors.details: The junta uses mining negotiations to assert sovereignty while facing pressure over political transition timelines. Contract uncertainty can deter investment even as the state demands greater control.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Raw-cashew exports dominate rural incomes, while processing and pricing remain heavily influenced by foreign traders and buyers. Limited infrastructure prevents the state from capturing more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security and illicit networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak coastal surveillance leaves fisheries and maritime routes vulnerable to illegal activity, including narcotics trafficking. External security assistance is useful but reinforces dependence on outside actors.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders remain important to major transport and energy projects, creating exposure to refinancing pressure and external policy conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa faces competition from regional corridors and pressure to preserve Kenyan control over strategic logistics assets while expanding trade links to inland markets.

frictionVectors.title: Water-resource dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue but leaves the kingdom dependent on South African infrastructure, demand, and treaty arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and fiscal vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned textile production and external trade preferences provide employment while exposing Lesotho to shifting supply chains and policy decisions made abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and agricultural concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms dominate much of the iron ore, rubber, and plantation economy, limiting domestic value capture and intensifying scrutiny of land, labor, and revenue terms.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport and maritime dependence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and shipping sector rely heavily on external operators and capital, making infrastructure access and concession oversight central sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Foreign patrons shape security and exports

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks can disrupt fields, terminals, and export flows, while foreign partners seek leverage over production and contracting.

frictionVectors.title: External security competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian, European, and regional interests remain entangled in Libya's security environment, constraining unified national control of territory and strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed operations in nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other minerals provide exports but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak power and transport networks increase reliance on external financiers and operators, complicating efforts to retain more value from mining and agricultural supply chains.

highlights: Fertilizer and fuel dependence constrains policy space

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and revenue capture
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in uranium, rare earths and other minerals, but limited state capacity creates risks that foreign operators capture disproportionate value. Contract transparency and local-processing demands remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-linked fiscal adjustment
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages limit sovereign room over fuel, fertilizer and infrastructure policy. Dependence on external lenders can translate into pressure for rapid liberalization and subsidy restraint.

highlights: Junta asserts control over gold and strategic resources
Russian security ties replace much Western engagement

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalism
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is demanding larger state participation and tighter oversight of industrial gold mining, increasing tension with international operators. Falling security and regulatory predictability threaten production and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-access dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support has reduced Western leverage but may create opaque arrangements around concessions, logistics and strategic infrastructure. Insurgent attacks continue to undermine state control of resource corridors.

highlights: Gas exports open a new strategic revenue stream
Iron ore remains exposed to external markets

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and international partners offers diversification, but revenue-sharing, local-content and maritime-security issues could limit domestic gains. Mauritania remains dependent on foreign technology and financing.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore logistics bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: The state relies heavily on foreign demand and investment for iron ore while rail and port capacity constrain expansion. Commodity-price swings can quickly weaken fiscal sovereignty and bargaining power.

highlights: Indian Ocean positioning raises infrastructure stakes

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is balancing commercial ties with India, China, Europe and Gulf actors around ports, logistics and maritime security. Infrastructure partnerships can generate leverage concerns even without formal military alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Financial-sector external scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: The offshore and investment-services sector faces continuing pressure over tax transparency, beneficial ownership and illicit-finance controls. Compliance reforms protect market access but narrow some avenues of sovereign economic maneuver.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables underpin strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries and renewable projects in Western Sahara remain exposed to legal and diplomatic challenges over consent and sovereignty. External recognition and investment partnerships strengthen Morocco's position but also intensify regional opposition.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, high-speed rail, green hydrogen and defense-industrial projects rely on European, Gulf, Chinese and other external capital. Rabat retains strong state direction, but financing and technology partners can shape strategic priorities.

highlights: LNG ambitions constrained by Cabo Delgado insecurity
Ports and mineral corridors attract competing foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado security and LNG restart
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency and dependence on external security support continue to limit state control over northern energy assets. LNG development offers major fiscal upside but risks enclave-style extraction if local benefits and security governance remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed investment in ports, railways, and mining corridors increases connectivity while giving external firms and neighboring states leverage over export infrastructure.

highlights: Critical minerals and offshore oil reshape strategic relevance
Green hydrogen strategy seeks domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of new energy assets
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate much of the capital and technology entering green hydrogen, uranium, lithium, and offshore oil projects. Namibia is seeking local-content and fiscal safeguards, but bargaining power remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics capacity bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, water, and electricity constraints could force greater reliance on foreign infrastructure operators and limit domestic processing of strategic resources.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over uranium and oil policy
Western rupture deepens reliance on Russia and regional partners

frictionVectors.title: Resource nationalism under sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating foreign mining relationships and asserting greater control over uranium and hydrocarbons. Reduced Western engagement may improve political autonomy but also limits financing, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and export vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Oil exports and major infrastructure depend on cross-border routes and cooperation with neighboring states. Insecurity, diplomatic disputes, and dependence on external contractors threaten reliable monetization of resources.

highlights: Oil theft and infrastructure decay keep production fragile

frictionVectors.title: Refinery and upstream control
frictionVectors.details: The Dangote refinery and renewed domestic refining capacity could reduce dependence on imported fuel and improve bargaining power. However, crude supply constraints and competition among state, private, and foreign operators remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta insecurity and oil theft
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, theft, spills, and community grievances continue to reduce state control over petroleum infrastructure. Foreign firms retain influence while the government struggles to convert resource wealth into secure, broad-based development.

highlights: Regional security role increases external scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and supply-chain leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is pursuing greater value addition in tin, tantalum, tungsten, and gold, but external buyers and processing networks still shape market access. Mineral-origin scrutiny linked to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo creates reputational and diplomatic risk.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo security entanglement
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security posture and alleged support for M23 have triggered pressure from the DRC, Western governments, and regional institutions. Cross-border tensions can disrupt trade, investment, and Kigali's effort to present itself as a stable logistics hub.

frictionVectors.title: Unresolved offshore licensing
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest in the joint development zone with Nigeria offers potential leverage but has yet to produce commercial output. Limited state capacity increases the risk of opaque concessions and weak bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, and other partners remain important for transport, energy, and public infrastructure. Financing needs constrain the government's ability to impose strict local-content or sovereignty conditions.

highlights: New oil and gas sovereignty push

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national control and transparency in offshore oil and gas projects while avoiding disruption to production and investor confidence. Disputes over contracts, local content, and revenue management remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Dakar and competing regional corridors attract investment from European, Gulf, Chinese, and Turkish actors. External financing can improve connectivity but may create long-term leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles balances Indian, European, Chinese, and other security and infrastructure interests in a strategically valuable maritime zone. Port access, maritime surveillance, and security cooperation require careful safeguards against dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Climate and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rising climate costs and tourism concentration limit fiscal autonomy and increase reliance on external finance. Blue bonds and conservation partnerships can strengthen resource control but may impose restrictive oversight conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports, but concession terms, tax collection, environmental damage, and local benefits continue to challenge sovereign control. Foreign operators retain substantial influence over production and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-backed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign partners support roads, energy, mining, and port-related projects, expanding connectivity while deepening creditor and contractor dependence. Weak procurement capacity raises concerns over transparency and strategic asset control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and coastline competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the UAE, Gulf states, and other actors compete for influence over ports, security arrangements, and maritime trade routes. Fragmented federal authority limits Mogadishu's ability to enforce consistent national terms.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource governance
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil and gas licensing is advancing amid unresolved federal-regional disputes and limited regulatory capacity. Without transparent revenue-sharing and environmental rules, new concessions could intensify political fragmentation and external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital remains important in platinum-group metals, manganese and logistics, while port and rail constraints limit South Africa's ability to capture full value from its mineral base.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity transition pressure
frictionVectors.details: Private generation and international climate finance are helping stabilize power supply, but they also dilute direct state control over strategic energy infrastructure.

highlights: Oil revenues remain the sovereignty bottleneck

frictionVectors.title: Oil corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on export routes through Sudan and foreign operators for production, transit and technical services, leaving state revenue exposed to regional conflict and pipeline disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Security-sector fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Political and armed factions retain influence over territory and commerce, constraining central control over natural resources and enabling external patrons to shape local power balances.

highlights: Gold and ports anchor external competition

frictionVectors.title: Gold-war economy
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed authorities and foreign-linked trading networks capture much of the gold economy, reducing transparent public revenue and financing continued conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access contest
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and prospective basing arrangements have become bargaining assets for outside powers, while fighting and political fragmentation limit Khartoum's effective control.

highlights: Ports and LNG raise strategic stakes

frictionVectors.title: LNG and extractive bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater domestic value and fiscal control from gas and mineral projects, but large-scale development still relies on foreign capital, technology and long-term offtake arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Transport-corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf and Western-linked financing compete around ports, railways and regional corridors, giving Tanzania leverage while creating pressure to balance strategic infrastructure partners.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's regional leverage, but dependence on foreign finance, shipping networks and security partnerships limits exclusive national control over trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate value-chain constraints
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources, yet processing, investment and market access constraints limit its ability to convert reserves into broader sovereign industrial power.

highlights: Phosphate and fiscal sovereignty under strain

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on European financial support and cooperation over migration control, giving Brussels significant leverage over domestic policy and budget priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import exposure
frictionVectors.details: High reliance on imported hydrocarbons and slow renewable deployment limits Tunisia's strategic autonomy, despite efforts to expand solar capacity and regional energy links.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The China-backed East African Crude Oil Pipeline remains central to Uganda's export strategy but faces Western political, environmental, and financial pressure, increasing dependence on a narrow group of external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Oil revenue and local-content tensions
frictionVectors.details: Uganda is seeking greater domestic value capture from petroleum development, while foreign operators, imported technology, and regional infrastructure retain substantial control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is leveraging interest from China, the United States, and Europe to secure investment in copper and cobalt, but competition risks leaving processing, pricing, and technology decisions abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and power bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito and regional transport corridors could diversify export routes, yet unreliable electricity and rail capacity continue to constrain Zambia's ability to capture more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese mining and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain major players in lithium, platinum, and other minerals, providing capital and infrastructure while concerns persist over limited transparency, local value addition, and revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Power shortages undermine beneficiation
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and dependence on regional imports weaken Zimbabwe's ability to process minerals domestically and increase the bargaining power of external investors.
